notes.title: 1.1 Meaning and Definition of Accounting; Need and Objectives
notes.content:
• Accounting is the art of recording, classifying, summarising (in a significant manner and in terms of money) transactions and events of a financial character, and interpreting the results thereof. (AICPA, 1941).
• American Accounting Association (AAA): "the process of identifying, measuring and communicating economic information to permit informed judgements and decisions by users of the information."
• Smith and Ashburne: "Accounting is the science of recording and classifying business transactions and events, primarily of a financial character, and the art of making significant summaries, analyses and interpretations of those transactions and events and communicating the results to persons who must make decisions or form judgements."
• Book-keeping vs Accounting: book-keeping is only the recording part (journal, ledger); accounting includes recording + classification + summarising + analysis + interpretation + communication.
[TABLE]
Basis | Book-keeping | Accounting
Scope | Recording and posting | Complete process including analysis and interpretation
Work done by | Clerical staff | Accountants
Stage | First stage | Next stage (uses bookkeeping data)
Skill | Little knowledge needed | Specialised knowledge
Decision making | No | Yes
[/TABLE]
• Features: economic (financial) events only; measured in money; systematic recording; summarising; analysis and interpretation; communication to users.
• Need for accounting: to maintain records (human memory is limited); to know profit or loss; to know the financial position (assets and liabilities); to provide information to users; to meet legal requirements (Companies Act, Income-tax Act, GST); to compare performance over years and with other firms; to help in decision making, planning and control; as evidence in disputes; to raise loans and attract investors.
• Objectives of accounting:
– Maintaining systematic records of all business transactions.
– Ascertaining profit or loss of the business (Income statement).
– Ascertaining financial position (Balance sheet).
– Providing information to users for decisions.
– Protecting business assets from misuse and fraud.
– Complying with legal requirements (taxation, auditing, company law).
– Facilitating comparison and control.
• Branches of accounting: Financial accounting (records transactions; prepares financial statements for outsiders); Cost accounting (ascertains and controls cost of products); Management accounting (provides information to management for planning and control).
• Users of accounting information: Internal: owners, management, employees. External: investors, creditors/ lenders (banks), customers, suppliers, government (tax authorities), regulators (SEBI, RBI), researchers, public.
• Functions: recording, classifying, summarising, analysing, interpreting, communicating.
• Advantages: replaces memory; helps in tax assessment; basis for legal evidence; facilitates sale of business and valuation; helps raise finance; detects errors and frauds; helps comparison.
• Limitations: records only monetary transactions; based on historical cost (ignores inflation); influenced by personal judgement (depreciation, stock valuation); does not show current market value; ignores qualitative factors (employee morale, goodwill unless purchased); can be window-dressed; interim reports are only estimates.

notes.title: 1.2 Accounting Concepts and Conventions
notes.content:
• Accounting concepts are the basic assumptions/ rules that guide recording. Conventions are customs/ traditions that guide the preparation of financial statements.
• Fundamental accounting assumptions (AS 1 / Ind AS 1): Going concern, Consistency, Accrual.
• Accounting concepts:
– 1. Business entity concept: the business is a separate entity from its owner; owner's capital is a liability of the business to the owner. Personal transactions of the owner are not recorded in business books (drawings are treated as a reduction of capital).
– 2. Money measurement concept: only transactions expressible in money are recorded (skill of workers is ignored).
– 3. Going concern concept: the business is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future; hence fixed assets are recorded at cost less depreciation, not at sale (liquidation) value; prepaid expenses are carried forward.
– 4. Accounting period concept: the life of the business is divided into periods (usually 12 months — financial year 1 April to 31 March in India) to measure profit.
– 5. Cost concept (historical cost): assets are recorded at their purchase cost, not market value.
– 6. Dual aspect concept: every transaction has two aspects — debit and credit; basis of double entry; Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
– 7. Revenue recognition (realisation) concept: revenue is recognised when earned (goods delivered/ services rendered), not when cash is received (AS 9).
– 8. Matching concept: expenses of a period are matched with the revenues of the same period; hence outstanding and prepaid expenses are adjusted.
– 9. Accrual concept: revenues and costs are recognised when they occur, not when cash is exchanged (accrual basis vs cash basis).
– 10. Objectivity (verifiability) concept: records should be supported by documents (vouchers, bills, invoices) and free from bias.
– 11. Full disclosure and 12. Materiality (also conventions).
• Accounting conventions:
– Consistency: same methods applied year after year (e.g. depreciation method), enabling comparison.
– Conservatism (prudence): anticipate no profits but provide for all possible losses — e.g. stock valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower; provision for doubtful debts.
– Materiality: only significant items need separate disclosure; insignificant items (small stationery) can be treated as expense.
– Full disclosure: all significant information must be disclosed in the financial statements (notes, contingent liabilities).
• Basis of accounting: cash basis (income/expense recorded on receipt/payment) vs accrual (mercantile) basis (recorded when earned/incurred). Companies must follow accrual basis.

notes.title: 1.3 Accounting Equation
notes.content:
• Accounting equation (balance sheet equation): Assets = Liabilities + Capital (Owner's equity) or Capital = Assets − Liabilities.
• Terms:
– Asset: resource owned by the business with future economic benefit — fixed/ non-current (land, building, machinery), current (cash, debtors, stock, bills receivable, prepaid expenses), tangible vs intangible (goodwill, patents), fictitious assets (preliminary expenses).
– Liability: obligation to outsiders — current (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft) and long-term (loans, debentures).
– Capital: amount invested by the owner. Drawings: withdrawal by owner for personal use. Revenue/income: inflow from sales/services. Expense: cost of earning revenue. Gain/loss: incidental. Debtors: persons who owe money. Creditors: persons to whom the business owes. Stock/inventory, Purchases, Sales, Discount (trade and cash), Bad debts.
• Extended equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital + Revenue − Expenses − Drawings. Capital = opening capital + profit − drawings.
• Effect of transactions (the equation always remains balanced):
[TABLE]
Transaction | Assets | Liabilities | Capital
Started business with cash Rs 1,00,000 | +1,00,000 | — | +1,00,000
Bought furniture for cash Rs 20,000 | +20,000 −20,000 | — | —
Purchased goods on credit Rs 30,000 | +30,000 | +30,000 | —
Paid creditor Rs 10,000 | −10,000 | −10,000 | —
Paid rent Rs 2,000 | −2,000 | — | −2,000
Owner withdrew Rs 5,000 | −5,000 | — | −5,000
Took loan from bank Rs 50,000 | +50,000 | +50,000 | —
[/TABLE]
• Example: Assets Rs 5,00,000; outside liabilities Rs 1,50,000 → Capital = Rs 3,50,000.

notes.title: 1.4 Accounting Systems and Process; Single Entry and Double Entry
notes.content:
• Accounting systems:
– Single entry system: an incomplete system where only personal accounts (debtors and creditors) and cash book are maintained; real and nominal accounts are not fully maintained; used by small traders; no trial balance; profit is found by the statement of affairs method (closing capital − opening capital + drawings).
– Double entry system (Luca Pacioli, 1494): every transaction has two aspects — a debit and an equal credit. Complete and scientific.
– Cash vs accrual systems.
• Features of double entry: two accounts affected; equal debit and credit; complete record of personal, real and nominal accounts; trial balance possible to test arithmetical accuracy; basis for final accounts.
• Advantages: complete record, arithmetic accuracy check, ascertains profit/loss and financial position, prevents frauds, helps comparison and tax assessment. Limitations: costlier; cannot detect all errors (compensating errors, errors of principle, omission); needs trained staff.
[TABLE]
Basis | Single Entry | Double Entry
Nature | Incomplete | Complete
Dual effect | Not recorded | Recorded
Accounts | Personal and cash only | Personal, real, nominal
Trial balance | Not possible | Possible
Profit | Statement of affairs method | Final accounts
Suitable for | Small traders | All organisations
[/TABLE]
• Types of accounts: Personal (persons, firms, companies, banks, e.g. Ram's A/c, Bank A/c, Capital A/c); Real (assets and property: Cash, Furniture, Building); Nominal (expenses, losses, incomes and gains: Rent, Salaries, Commission received).
• Accounting process (cycle): identification of transactions → vouchers/source documents → journal (primary book) → ledger posting → balancing → trial balance → adjusting entries → final accounts (trading, P&L, balance sheet) → closing entries → opening entries for the next year.
• Accounting cycle (steps): 1. Identify and analyse transactions; 2. Record in journal/ subsidiary books; 3. Post to ledger; 4. Prepare trial balance; 5. Pass adjusting entries; 6. Prepare adjusted trial balance; 7. Prepare financial statements; 8. Pass closing entries; 9. Post-closing trial balance/ opening entries.

notes.title: 1.5 Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP)
notes.content:
• GAAP: the common set of accounting principles, standards and procedures that companies follow in preparing financial statements — ensures consistency, comparability, transparency and reliability.
• Sources in India: Companies Act, 2013 (Section 129, Schedule III — format of financial statements; Section 133 — notified standards); Accounting Standards (AS) issued by the ICAI (Institute of Chartered Accountants of India); Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) converged with IFRS (issued by IASB) — applicable to listed and larger companies; ICAI guidance notes; SEBI regulations; Income Computation and Disclosure Standards (ICDS) for tax.
• Some Accounting Standards: AS 1 Disclosure of accounting policies; AS 2 Inventories; AS 3 Cash flow statements; AS 6 Depreciation Accounting; AS 9 Revenue recognition; AS 10 Property, plant & equipment; AS 14; AS 16 Borrowing costs; AS 26 Intangible assets. Ind AS 1 Presentation; Ind AS 2 Inventories; Ind AS 16 PPE; Ind AS 115 Revenue from contracts with customers.
• Global: IFRS (IASB), US GAAP (FASB). National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) monitors compliance in India.
• Principles: (see concepts above) — plus fair presentation, substance over form, going concern, accrual, comparability, relevance and reliability, understandability.

notes.title: 1.6 Accounting Cycle and Final Accounts — Preview
notes.content:
• Financial statements = Income statement (Trading and Profit & Loss A/c) + Balance sheet (+ cash flow statement and notes for companies).
• Capital expenditure (benefit for more than one year — purchase of machinery) vs revenue expenditure (benefit for one year — wages, rent) vs deferred revenue expenditure (large expense, benefit over several years — heavy advertisement).
• Capital receipts (sale of assets, capital introduced, loans) vs revenue receipts (sales, commission, interest).

notes.title: 2.1 Meaning and Systems of Book-Keeping
notes.content:
• Book-keeping: the art of recording business transactions in a systematic manner in the books of accounts. (R.N. Carter: "Book-keeping is the science and art of correctly recording in books of account all those business transactions that result in transfer of money or money's worth.")
• Objectives: to maintain permanent records; to find results (profit/loss); to know financial position; to help in preparation of final accounts and taxation; to protect assets.
• Features: records only financial transactions; chronological; based on vouchers; first stage of accounting.
• Systems of book-keeping:
– Single entry system (incomplete; see Unit 1).
– Double entry system (complete; each transaction has two effects).
– Cameral system (government accounting, Germany) and Italian system (earlier name of double entry).
• Double entry principle: "For every debit there is an equal credit" — total debits = total credits.
• Meaning of debit and credit: debit (Dr) is the left side of an account; credit (Cr) is the right side. Debit does not mean "bad" — it is only a side. Abbreviation: Dr (debit), Cr (credit), A/c (account), To/By used in ledger.

notes.title: 2.2 Classification of Accounts and Golden Rules
notes.content:
• Traditional (English) approach — three types:
– Personal accounts: relate to persons/ organisations. Natural (Ram, Shyam), Artificial (companies, banks, firms, clubs), Representative (outstanding salary — represents the employee; prepaid insurance; capital; drawings).
– Real accounts: relate to assets/properties. Tangible (cash, furniture, building, stock) and Intangible (goodwill, patents, trademarks).
– Nominal accounts: relate to expenses, losses, incomes and gains (rent, wages, salaries, interest paid, discount allowed, commission earned, interest received, discount received). Fictitious in nature.
• Golden rules (English system):
[TABLE]
Type of account | Rule | Meaning
Personal | Debit the receiver, Credit the giver | The person who receives a benefit is debited; the person who gives it is credited
Real | Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out | Increase in an asset is debited; decrease credited
Nominal | Debit all expenses and losses, Credit all incomes and gains | Expenses/losses on debit side; incomes/gains on credit side
[/TABLE]
• Modern (American) approach — five categories: Assets, Liabilities, Capital, Revenue (Income), Expenses.
[TABLE]
Category | Increase | Decrease
Assets | Debit | Credit
Expenses (and losses) | Debit | Credit
Liabilities | Credit | Debit
Capital | Credit | Debit
Revenue (incomes and gains) | Credit | Debit
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Category | Increase | Decrease
Drawings | Debit | Credit
[/TABLE]
• Mnemonic-free summary: the left side (debit) shows assets, expenses and drawings; the right side (credit) shows liabilities, capital and income.
• Differences between English and American systems: English approach classifies into personal, real and nominal with the golden rules; American approach uses the accounting equation (assets, liabilities, capital, income, expenses) with debit/credit rules for each. Both give identical debit/credit results.
• Examples:
[TABLE]
Transaction | Accounts involved | Debit | Credit
Started business with cash Rs 50,000 | Cash (real), Capital (personal) | Cash | Capital
Bought furniture for cash | Furniture (real), Cash (real) | Furniture | Cash
Purchased goods on credit from Ram | Purchases (nominal), Ram (personal) | Purchases | Ram
Sold goods to Shyam on credit | Shyam (personal), Sales (nominal) | Shyam | Sales
Paid rent | Rent (nominal), Cash (real) | Rent | Cash
Received commission | Cash (real), Commission (nominal) | Cash | Commission received
Withdrew cash for personal use | Drawings (personal), Cash (real) | Drawings | Cash
Paid wages outstanding | Outstanding wages (personal), Cash (real) | Outstanding wages | Cash
Received interest from bank | Bank (personal), Interest (nominal) | Bank | Interest received
Depreciation charged on machinery | Depreciation (nominal), Machinery (real) | Depreciation | Machinery
Bad debts written off | Bad debts (nominal), Debtor (personal) | Bad debts | Debtor
Cash discount allowed to a customer | Discount allowed (nominal), Debtor | Discount allowed | Customer
Goods returned to supplier | Supplier (personal), Purchases Return (nominal) | Supplier | Purchases return
Goods returned by customer | Sales return (nominal), Customer (personal) | Sales return | Customer
[/TABLE]
• Capital and drawings accounts are treated as personal accounts (owner = a person). Drawings of goods are credited to Purchases A/c (or Drawings of goods).
• Vouchers/ source documents: cash memo, invoice, debit note, credit note, receipt, pay-in-slip, cheque, salary sheet; debit note — sent by buyer to seller for returns (buyer debits seller); credit note — sent by the seller to the buyer for returns by customer (seller credits customer).

notes.title: 2.3 Debit and Credit under English and American Systems — Application
notes.content:
• English system: analyse each transaction into the two accounts, determine nature of each, and apply the golden rule to each.
• American system: determine whether the item is asset/ liability/ capital/ revenue/ expense; apply the increase/ decrease rule.
• Example: Purchased machinery on credit Rs 40,000. English: Machinery (real) — comes in, debit; Creditor (personal) — giver, credit. American: Machinery (asset) increases — debit; Creditor (liability) increases — credit.
• Example: Paid Rs 5,000 to creditor. Creditor (personal) — receiver, debit; Cash (real) — goes out, credit. American: liability decreases — debit; asset decreases — credit.
• Example: Received Rs 3,000 as rent. Cash comes in — debit; Rent received (income) — credit.
• Example: Goods taken by owner: Drawings Dr, Purchases Cr (at cost).

notes.group_name: Unit 3: Book of Prime Entry — Journal
notes.title: 3.1 Journal: Meaning, Features, Objectives and Advantages
notes.content:
• Journal: the book of original (prime) entry in which transactions are first recorded chronologically (date wise) with their debit and credit effects, along with a short narration. The word comes from French "jour" meaning day. The act of recording is journalising; the entry is a journal entry.
• Features: chronological; first record; each entry shows debit and credit accounts; includes narration (brief explanation); dual aspect recorded; source of ledger posting; each transaction recorded after a voucher.
• Objectives: to record all transactions in order; to analyse each transaction into debit and credit; to make posting in the ledger easy; to provide an explanation (narration); to reduce errors.
• Advantages: chronological record; analytical (shows both accounts); narration helps understanding; helps in detection of errors and frauds; reduces mistakes in ledger posting; evidence for disputes; saves time in ledger posting.
• Disadvantages: time-consuming and costly for big businesses (hence subsidiary books are used); repeated writing of the same account name; not suitable for voluminous transactions.
• Format of journal:
[TABLE]
Date | Particulars | L.F. | Debit (Rs) | Credit (Rs)
2026 Jan 1 | Cash A/c Dr. |  | 1,00,000 |
| To Capital A/c |  |  | 1,00,000
| (Being business started with cash) |  |  |
[/TABLE]
• Columns: Date; Particulars (accounts with "Dr." and "To"; narration in brackets starting with "Being"); L.F. (ledger folio) — page number of the ledger account after posting; Debit amount; Credit amount.
• Rules for journalising: (1) identify accounts; (2) classify (personal/real/nominal); (3) apply golden rules; (4) debit account written first with "Dr."; credit account on the next line, indented with "To"; (5) amount in the proper column; (6) narration.
• Types of journal entries: Simple entry (one debit and one credit); Compound entry (more than two accounts: e.g. one debit, many credits; many debits, one credit); Opening entry (assets Dr, liabilities and capital Cr — at start of the new year); Closing entries (transfer nominal accounts to trading and P&L at year end); Adjusting entries (outstanding/prepaid/depreciation etc.); Transfer entries (from one account to another); Rectification entries (correct errors).
• Trade discount vs cash discount: trade discount (reduction in list price; not recorded in books — record only the net amount) vs cash discount (for prompt payment; recorded as discount allowed/received).

notes.group_name: Unit 3: Book of Prime Entry — Journal
notes.title: 3.2 Recording Transactions in Journal — Illustrations
notes.content:
• Illustration — Journalise the following in the books of Mr. Rao:
– Jan 1: Commenced business with cash Rs 1,00,000.
– Jan 2: Bought furniture for cash Rs 20,000.
– Jan 3: Purchased goods from Ram on credit Rs 30,000.
– Jan 5: Sold goods to Shyam on credit Rs 25,000.
– Jan 8: Paid rent Rs 2,000.
– Jan 10: Received Rs 24,000 from Shyam in full settlement of his account (discount Rs 1,000).
– Jan 12: Paid Rs 29,000 to Ram in full settlement of Rs 30,000.
– Jan 15: Withdrew cash Rs 5,000 for personal use.
– Jan 20: Took goods costing Rs 3,000 for personal use.
– Jan 31: Salary outstanding Rs 4,000.
[TABLE]
Date | Particulars | Dr (Rs) | Cr (Rs)
Jan 1 | Cash A/c Dr. / To Capital A/c | 1,00,000 | 1,00,000
Jan 2 | Furniture A/c Dr. / To Cash A/c | 20,000 | 20,000
Jan 3 | Purchases A/c Dr. / To Ram | 30,000 | 30,000
Jan 5 | Shyam Dr. / To Sales A/c | 25,000 | 25,000
Jan 8 | Rent A/c Dr. / To Cash A/c | 2,000 | 2,000
Jan 10 | Cash A/c Dr. 24,000; Discount Allowed A/c Dr. 1,000 / To Shyam | 25,000 | 25,000
Jan 12 | Ram Dr. 30,000 / To Cash A/c 29,000; To Discount Received A/c 1,000 | 30,000 | 30,000
Jan 15 | Drawings A/c Dr. / To Cash A/c | 5,000 | 5,000
Jan 20 | Drawings A/c Dr. / To Purchases A/c | 3,000 | 3,000
Jan 31 | Salary A/c Dr. / To Outstanding Salary A/c | 4,000 | 4,000
[/TABLE]
• Other typical entries:
– Bad debts written off: Bad Debts A/c Dr. / To Debtor's A/c. Bad debts recovered: Cash A/c Dr. / To Bad Debts Recovered A/c.
– Goods destroyed by fire (uninsured): Loss by Fire A/c Dr. / To Purchases A/c (insured: Insurance Claim A/c Dr. for the claim).
– Goods given as free samples/charity: Advertisement (or Charity) A/c Dr. / To Purchases A/c.
– Sale of old asset at profit/loss: Cash Dr.; Loss Dr./ To Asset; To Profit.
– Depreciation: Depreciation A/c Dr. / To Asset A/c.
– Interest on capital: Interest on Capital A/c Dr. / To Capital A/c. Interest on drawings: Drawings A/c Dr. / To Interest on Drawings A/c.
– Opening entry: Assets (Cash, Stock, Debtors) Dr. / To Liabilities (Creditors), To Capital (balancing figure) — the account name is "Balance b/d" in narration.
– Purchase of asset on credit: Asset Dr. / To Supplier. Loan taken: Cash/Bank Dr. / To Loan A/c.
– Compound entry — Salary paid and rent paid together: Salary A/c Dr.; Rent A/c Dr. / To Cash A/c.
– Goods sold at list price Rs 10,000 less 10% trade discount, 5% cash discount on payment: sale recorded at Rs 9,000 (net); cash received Rs 8,550 with discount Rs 450.

notes.group_name: Unit 3: Book of Prime Entry — Journal
notes.title: 3.3 Problems on Journalising
notes.content:
• Steps: (1) read the transaction; (2) identify the two (or more) accounts; (3) classify and apply rules; (4) record the date and narration.
• Problem — Opening entry: Mr. Gupta's position on 1 April: Cash Rs 15,000; Stock Rs 40,000; Debtors Rs 25,000; Furniture Rs 20,000; Creditors Rs 30,000; Bank loan Rs 20,000. Capital = (15,000 + 40,000 + 25,000 + 20,000) − (30,000 + 20,000) = 1,00,000 − 50,000 = Rs 50,000. Entry: Cash Dr. 15,000; Stock Dr. 40,000; Debtors Dr. 25,000; Furniture Dr. 20,000 / To Creditors 30,000; To Bank loan 20,000; To Capital 50,000.
• Problem — Closing entries: Transfer Sales (Rs 2,00,000) to Trading A/c: Sales A/c Dr. / To Trading A/c. Transfer Purchases to Trading: Trading A/c Dr. / To Purchases A/c. Transfer expenses to P&L: P&L A/c Dr. / To Salaries, Rent, etc. Transfer net profit to Capital: P&L A/c Dr. / To Capital A/c.
• Cash discount illustration: goods sold to X for Rs 10,000; X pays within the time and is allowed 2% discount: Cash Dr. 9,800; Discount Allowed Dr. 200 / To X 10,000.

notes.group_name: Unit 4: Books of Second Entry — Ledger
notes.title: 4.1 Ledger: Meaning, Features and Distinction from Journal
notes.content:
• Ledger: the principal book of accounts in which transactions recorded in the journal/ subsidiary books are classified and posted account-wise. It is the book of second (final) entry. "The ledger is the book which contains all the accounts" — it is called the "king of all books".
• Features: each account has a separate page/ folio; it is classified (account-wise) not chronological; each account has two sides — debit (left) and credit (right); derived from journal; basis for the trial balance and final accounts; maintained as bound book or loose-leaf/computerised.
• Types of ledgers: General ledger (all real and nominal accounts), Debtors' (sales) ledger and Creditors' (bought) ledger (personal accounts), private ledger (confidential accounts such as capital, drawings, profit).
• Format of a ledger account (T-form):
• Left (debit) side: Date | Particulars (To …) | J.F. | Amount (Rs). Right (credit) side: Date | Particulars (By …) | J.F. | Amount (Rs).
• "To" is used on the debit side and "By" on the credit side in the particulars column; the J.F. (journal folio) column records the journal page number.
• Distinction between journal and ledger:
[TABLE]
Basis | Journal | Ledger
Nature | Book of original/first entry | Book of second/final entry
Recording | Chronological (date-wise) | Classified (account-wise)
Basis | Vouchers/ source documents | Journal entries
Narration | Given | Not given
Columns | Date, particulars, L.F., Dr, Cr | Two sides: Dr and Cr, each with date, particulars, J.F., amount
Accounts | Shows both accounts affected | Shows one account at a time
Balancing | No balancing | Accounts are balanced
Purpose | To record transactions | To summarise and prepare trial balance
[/TABLE]

notes.group_name: Unit 4: Books of Second Entry — Ledger
notes.title: 4.2 Posting and Balancing
notes.content:
• Posting: the process of transferring the journal entries to the respective ledger accounts.
• Steps of posting: (1) open an account for each account named in the journal; (2) for the debit account in the journal, record the date, "To" + name of the other (credit) account, and amount on the debit (left) side; (3) for the credit account record the date, "By" + the name of the debit account, amount on the credit (right) side; (4) enter the journal folio in the ledger and the ledger folio in the journal; (5) for compound entries, use "To Sundries" or "By Sundries" or each account.
• Balancing: after posting, the totals of the two sides are found, and the difference — balance — is inserted on the smaller side as "By balance c/d" (if debit side is bigger — the account has debit balance) or "To balance c/d" (if credit side is bigger); totals are equal; balance is brought down on the opposite side: "To balance b/d" (debit balance) or "By balance b/d" (credit balance).
• Nature of balances: Debit balance — assets, expenses, losses, debtors, drawings. Credit balance — liabilities, capital, incomes, creditors. Cash account never shows a credit balance; (Bank account shows a credit balance only if overdrawn).
• Nominal accounts (expenses/incomes) are generally not carried forward; they are closed by transfer to Trading/P&L at the end of the year.
• Posting of special items: discount allowed/ received accounts are posted from the cash book totals; sales returns/purchase returns; opening balances.
• Illustration — Cash account of Mr. Rao (from the journal entries of Unit 3):
[TABLE]
Dr. side (Rs) | Cr. side (Rs)
To Capital 1,00,000 | By Furniture 20,000
To Shyam 24,000 | By Rent 2,000
| By Ram 29,000
| By Drawings 5,000
| By Balance c/d 68,000
Total 1,24,000 | Total 1,24,000
[/TABLE]
• Other account balances: Furniture Dr 20,000; Purchases Dr 30,000 less Cr 3,000 (drawings) = Dr 27,000; Sales Cr 25,000; Shyam: Dr 25,000, Cr cash 24,000, Cr discount 1,000 = Nil; Ram: Cr 30,000, Dr cash 29,000, Dr discount 1,000 = Nil; Rent Dr 2,000; Drawings Dr 8,000; Salary Dr 4,000; Outstanding salary Cr 4,000; Discount allowed Dr 1,000; Discount received Cr 1,000; Capital Cr 1,00,000.

notes.group_name: Unit 4: Books of Second Entry — Ledger
notes.title: 4.3 Trial Balance and Verification of Arithmetical Accuracy
notes.content:
• Trial balance: a statement of all ledger balances (debit and credit) as on a given date prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books. If the totals agree, the books are arithmetically correct (but not necessarily error-free).
• Objectives: to check arithmetical accuracy; to help prepare final accounts; to locate errors; to provide a summary of ledger accounts; to help in preparing adjusted accounts.
• Methods: Balance method (most common; list balances), Total method (list totals of debit and credit sides of each account), Total-cum-balance method (both).
• Format:
[TABLE]
Sl | Name of account | L.F. | Debit balance (Rs) | Credit balance (Rs)
1 | Cash |  | 68,000 |
2 | Capital |  |  | 1,00,000
[/TABLE]
• Rules of preparing: list debit balances (assets, expenses, drawings, losses, debtors) in the debit column; credit balances (liabilities, capital, incomes, creditors) in the credit column; closing stock appears in the trial balance only if given as the adjustment — opening stock is given in the TB; if the closing stock is given in the trial balance itself (after adjusting purchases), it is shown only in the balance sheet, not in the trading account.
• Trial balance of Mr. Rao (from the example):
[TABLE]
Account | Debit (Rs) | Credit (Rs)
Cash | 68,000 |
Furniture | 20,000 |
Purchases (net) | 27,000 |
Rent | 2,000 |
Discount allowed | 1,000 |
Drawings | 8,000 |
Salary | 4,000 |
Capital |  | 1,00,000
Sales |  | 25,000
Discount received |  | 1,000
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Account | Debit (Rs) | Credit (Rs)
Outstanding salary |  | 4,000
Total | 1,30,000 | 1,30,000
[/TABLE]
• Errors not disclosed by the trial balance: errors of omission (complete), commission (wrong account — same amount), compensating errors, errors of principle (capital treated as revenue), duplication/ original entry errors, wrong amount in both journal and ledger.
• Errors disclosed: one-sided posting, wrong totalling, wrong balancing, wrong carry-forward, posting different amounts on the two sides, omitting a balance from the trial balance.
• If the trial balance does not agree: the difference is temporarily put in Suspense Account (see Unit 6).
• Limitations: agreement of the trial balance is not a conclusive proof of accuracy; it does not show profit; errors of principle remain.
• Trial balance vs balance sheet: TB is a statement of balances to check accuracy (prepared before adjustments; includes nominal accounts) whereas the balance sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities (prepared after adjustments).

notes.title: 5.1 Meaning and Features of Subsidiary Books
notes.content:
• Subsidiary books (special journals): books in which similar transactions are recorded together — the journal is subdivided according to the nature of the transactions. They are books of original entry; they reduce the work of the journal and ledger posting, allow division of labour, and give quick reference and speedy posting (only totals are posted).
• Advantages: division of work; saves time and labour (periodic totals posted); reduces errors; helps in locating errors and fraud; more detail; makes the trial balance quick; specialised staff.
• Different subsidiary books:
– Purchases Book (Purchase Journal): only credit purchases of goods (merchandise for resale).
– Sales Book (Sales Journal): only credit sales of goods.
– Purchases Returns Book (Returns Outward): goods returned to suppliers (debit note).
– Sales Returns Book (Returns Inward): goods returned by customers (credit note).
– Bills Receivable Book and Bills Payable Book: bills of exchange/ promissory notes received/ accepted.
– Cash Book (single column, double column, three column; petty cash book).
– Journal Proper: for all other transactions not covered above (opening, closing, adjusting, rectification entries, credit purchase of assets).
• Documents used: invoice, cash memo, debit note, credit note, bill.

notes.title: 5.2 Purchases Book, Sales Book and Returns Books
notes.content:
• Purchases Book format: Date | Invoice no. | Particulars (supplier) | L.F. | Details (Rs) | Amount (Rs). Trade discount is deducted from the invoice price and the net amount is entered. Only goods (for resale) on credit; cash purchases go to the cash book; credit purchase of an asset (e.g. furniture) goes to the journal proper.
– Posting: each supplier's account is credited (individually with the invoice amount); the total of the purchases book is debited to Purchases A/c at the end of the period.
• Sales Book format: same as the purchases book, with the customer's name. Posting: each customer's account is debited; the total of the sales book is credited to Sales A/c.
• Purchases Returns Book: Posting: supplier's account is debited; total is credited to Purchases Returns A/c. Sales Returns Book: customer's account is credited; the total is debited to Sales Returns A/c.
• Illustration — Purchases Book of Mr. Rao (Jan 2026):
[TABLE]
Date | Supplier | Details | Amount (Rs)
Jan 3 | Ram | 100 units @ Rs 300, less 10% trade discount | 27,000
Jan 12 | Mohan | 50 units @ Rs 400 | 20,000
Jan 20 | Sohan | 80 units @ Rs 250, less 5% trade discount | 19,000
| Total (debit to Purchases A/c) |  | 66,000
[/TABLE]
• Illustration — Sales Book of Mr. Rao:
[TABLE]
Date | Customer | Details | Amount (Rs)
Jan 5 | Shyam | 60 units @ Rs 500 | 30,000
Jan 15 | Gopal | 40 units @ Rs 500, less 10% discount | 18,000
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Date | Customer | Details | Amount (Rs)
| Total (credit to Sales A/c) |  | 48,000
[/TABLE]
• GST invoices: under GST, invoices show CGST, SGST/IGST separately (input tax credit); purchases and sales books often have separate columns for the tax.
• Contra of returns: returns are deducted from the respective totals at the time of final accounts (or net purchases = purchases − returns).

notes.title: 5.3 Bills Receivable and Bills Payable Books
notes.content:
• Bill of exchange: a written, unconditional order by the drawer directing the drawee to pay a certain sum on demand or on a fixed date to the payee. Parties: drawer, drawee (acceptor), payee. Promissory note: an unconditional promise by the maker to pay.
• Bills Receivable Book: records all bills received from customers. Entries: Bills Receivable A/c Dr. / To Debtor; Posting: debit Bills Receivable A/c (total); credit the drawer/ debtor individually.
• Bills Payable Book: records all bills accepted for suppliers. Entry: Creditor Dr. / To Bills Payable A/c. Posting: debit the creditors individually; credit Bills Payable A/c (total).
• Dishonour, discounting, endorsement, retirement of bills; days of grace — 3 days are added to the due date for bills other than payable on demand (as per Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881).

notes.title: 5.4 Cash Book — Single, Double and Three Column; Petty Cash
notes.content:
• Cash book: a book of original entry and also ledger account of cash (both a subsidiary book and a principal book). Records all cash receipts (debit side) and cash payments (credit side) in chronological order. It is balanced like a ledger; the closing balance is cash in hand (always a debit balance).
• Types:
– Single column cash book: has only cash column (both sides).
– Double column cash book: cash column + discount column OR cash + bank column.
– Three column cash book: Discount, Cash and Bank columns on both sides.
– Petty cash book: records small payments.
• Three column cash book — rules: left (debit) side — receipts; right (credit) side — payments. The discount column on the debit side = Discount allowed (expense/loss to the business); the credit side discount column = Discount received (gain). Discount columns are only totalled, not balanced; the totals are posted: debit-side total to Discount Allowed A/c (Dr) and credit-side total to Discount Received A/c (Cr).
• Contra entry: a transaction affecting both cash and bank (e.g. cash deposited in bank; cash withdrawn from bank for office use). Recorded on both sides of the cash book, with the letter "C" in the L.F. column; no ledger posting.
– Cash deposited into bank: Bank column — debit; Cash column — credit. Cash withdrawn from bank for office: Cash column — debit; Bank column — credit.
• Cheques: cheque received and deposited on the same day: bank column debit. Cheque issued: bank column credit. Dishonoured cheque: entry reversed (Debtor Dr / To Bank).
• Posting from the cash book: Debit side items → credit the respective account in the ledger (to the "By" side); Credit side items → debit the respective account. In the cash book, the particulars show the "other" account (the account to be credited/debited).
• Illustration — Three column cash book:
– Opening: Cash Rs 5,000; Bank Rs 20,000. Transactions: sold goods for cash Rs 10,000; deposited cash Rs 6,000 in bank; received cheque from A Rs 8,000 (discount allowed Rs 200) and deposited; paid B by cheque Rs 5,000 (discount received Rs 100); paid salaries in cash Rs 2,000; withdrew from bank Rs 1,500 for office use.
[TABLE]
DEBIT SIDE | Discount | Cash | Bank
To Balance b/d |  | 5,000 | 20,000
To Sales |  | 10,000 |
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
DEBIT SIDE | Discount | Cash | Bank
To Cash (C) |  |  | 6,000
To A | 200 |  | 8,000
To Bank (C) |  | 1,500 |
Total | 200 | 16,500 | 34,000
CREDIT SIDE | Discount | Cash | Bank
By Bank (C) |  | 6,000 |
By B | 100 |  | 5,000
By Salaries |  | 2,000 |
By Cash (C) |  |  | 1,500
By Balance c/d |  | 8,500 | 27,500
Total | 100 | 16,500 | 34,000
[/TABLE]
• Bank column: a credit balance in the bank column means an overdraft.
• Single column illustration: start with cash 3,000; receipts: sales 5,000; payments: purchases 2,000; balance 6,000.
• Petty cash book: maintained by the petty cashier to record small expenses (postage, stationery, conveyance, tea) so that the main cashier is relieved.
– Imprest system: the petty cashier is given a fixed sum (imprest) at the beginning of the period; at the end of the period, the amount spent is reimbursed so that the imprest is restored. Advantage: better control, minimises fraud.
– Analytical (columnar) petty cash book: has a receipts column, a total payments column and analysis columns (postage, stationery, travelling, sundry) — totals posted to ledger accounts.
– Illustration: imprest Rs 2,000; payments: stationery 400; postage 300; conveyance 250; miscellaneous 150. Total spent = 1,100; reimbursement = Rs 1,100; closing balance = Rs 900 (restored to 2,000 after reimbursement).

notes.title: 5.5 Balancing and Posting to Ledger and Journal Proper
notes.content:
• Balancing the cash book: total each side; the difference — balance c/d on the smaller side; balance b/d on the opposite side in the next period. The cash column never has a credit balance; the bank column may (overdraft).
• Journal proper entries (examples): Opening entries; Closing entries; Adjusting entries (outstanding, prepaid, accrued, depreciation, provision); Transfer entries; Rectification entries; credit purchase/ sale of assets; bad debts; discount adjustments; drawings of goods; goods lost by fire; interest on capital/drawings; endorsement/ dishonour of bills.
• Posting to ledger: purchases book (creditors cr, purchases dr by total); sales book (debtors dr, sales cr); cash book (as above); contra entries (not posted).
• Differences between cash book and cash account: the cash book is both a book of original entry and a ledger; no separate cash account is needed.

notes.title: 6.1 Errors in Accounting: Meaning and Types
notes.content:
• Error: a mistake in recording, posting, totalling or balancing that leads to wrong accounts. Errors may be unintentional (clerical) or intentional (fraud).
• Types (on the basis of nature):
– 1. Errors of omission: transaction is completely omitted (complete omission) or partly omitted (e.g. recorded in the journal but not posted to the ledger, or posted on one side only). Complete omission — does not affect the trial balance. Partial omission (one-sided) — affects the trial balance.
– 2. Errors of commission: errors in recording/ posting/ totalling/ balancing — e.g. wrong amount, wrong side, posting to the wrong person's account (same type of account), wrong casting. May or may not affect the trial balance (posting to the wrong account does not; wrong amount on one side does).
– 3. Errors of principle: a violation of accounting principles — capital expenditure treated as revenue (or vice versa), or confusing personal, real and nominal accounts. Does not affect the trial balance.
– 4. Compensating errors: errors that cancel each other (one account excess debited, another excess credited by the same amount). Does not affect the trial balance.
– 5. Errors of original entry (wrong amount in books of original entry): wrong amount recorded in the original entry; both debit and credit have the same wrong amount — trial balance agrees.
– 6. Errors of duplication: the same transaction recorded twice.
– 7. Errors of casting/ wrong totalling: overcasting or undercasting of subsidiary books or ledger accounts — affects the trial balance.
• Classified by effect on trial balance: errors not affecting the trial balance (two-sided errors): complete omission, principle, compensating, original entry, posting to the wrong account (same side), wrong debits and credits of equal amounts. Errors affecting the trial balance (one-sided errors): posting on one side only, wrong amount posted to one side only, wrong totalling or balancing, omission of a balance from TB, wrong carry forward, opening balance wrongly brought forward.
• Causes: carelessness, lack of knowledge, confusion between principles, fatigue, fraud, poor internal control.
• Locating errors: compare the TB totals, check if the difference is divisible by 9 (transposition: digits reversed, e.g. 63 recorded as 36 — difference 27, divisible by 9; slide: e.g. 540 as 5,400), check if the difference equals a single posting, or half the difference equals an entry posted to the wrong side (difference ÷ 2), re-add, compare the ledger and subsidiary books, check opening balances.

notes.title: 6.2 Agreement of Trial Balance; Suspense Account
notes.content:
• Suspense account: a temporary account opened to record the difference when the trial balance does not tally; it is shown in the trial balance to make both sides equal, and removed after errors are located and rectified. If the difference is on the debit side short — Suspense A/c is debited in TB; if the credit side is short — Suspense A/c is credited.
• Need: to prepare final accounts without waiting for error location; finally, the suspense account will have a nil balance when all errors are found. If the suspense balance remains after rectification, it is shown in the balance sheet (debit balance on the assets side; credit balance on the liabilities side).
• Difference between suspense and "difference in books".

notes.title: 6.3 Rectification of Errors
notes.content:
• When errors are detected: (a) before the preparation of the trial balance/ same accounting year — rectify by a correcting entry/ simply correct the entries; (b) after the trial balance but before final accounts — through suspense account for one-sided errors; (c) after the final accounts are prepared (next year) — through the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account for errors affecting nominal accounts of the previous year.
• Steps for rectification: (1) identify the error; (2) ascertain the wrong entry passed; (3) find the correct entry; (4) find the rectifying entry — by cancelling the wrong effect and passing the correct entry. Consider what accounts are wrongly debited/credited.
• Rectification rules:
– One-sided errors (affect TB): use Suspense A/c — if a debit was omitted → debit the proper account and credit Suspense; if a credit was omitted → credit the proper account and debit Suspense.
– Two-sided errors (do not affect TB): rectify without suspense; pass an entry that reverses wrong and posts correct.
• Examples of rectification entries:
[TABLE]
Error | Rectifying entry
Goods sold to Mohan Rs 5,000 not recorded at all | Mohan Dr. 5,000 / To Sales 5,000
Purchase of furniture Rs 10,000 debited to Purchases A/c (principle) | Furniture A/c Dr. 10,000 / To Purchases A/c 10,000
Cash received from X Rs 2,000 posted to the debit of X's account (instead of credit) | Suspense A/c Dr. 4,000 / To X 4,000
Rent paid Rs 3,000 posted to the credit of rent account (instead of debit) | Rent A/c Dr. 6,000 / To Suspense A/c 6,000
Salary Rs 5,000 debited to Rent A/c | Salary A/c Dr. 5,000 / To Rent A/c 5,000
Goods purchased from A Rs 4,000 credited to B's account by mistake | B Dr. 4,000 / To A 4,000
Purchase book overcast by Rs 1,000 | Suspense A/c Dr. 1,000 / To Purchases A/c 1,000
Sales book undercast by Rs 2,000 | Suspense A/c Dr. 2,000 / To Sales A/c 2,000
Wages paid for installation of machinery Rs 5,000 debited to Wages | Machinery A/c Dr. 5,000 / To Wages A/c 5,000
Sale of old machine for Rs 7,000 credited to Sales | Sales A/c Dr. 7,000 / To Machinery A/c 7,000
Drawings of Rs 3,000 debited to Salary A/c | Drawings A/c Dr. 3,000 / To Salary A/c 3,000
Goods returned by customer Rs 500 not recorded | Sales Returns A/c Dr. 500 / To Customer 500
[/TABLE]
• Understanding suspense direction: if the credit side of the TB was short, a credit of the same amount is put in Suspense (credit balance); rectification of undercast sales credits Sales and debits Suspense, clearing it. If the debit side was short, debit Suspense; rectification credits Suspense.
• Illustration — Suspense account: TB difference of Rs 5,000 (credit total exceeded debit — suspense debited). Errors found: (a) Rent paid Rs 3,000 was not posted to the Rent account (debit omitted); (b) Purchases book undercast by Rs 2,000. Rectification: Rent A/c Dr 3,000 / To Suspense A/c 3,000; Purchases A/c Dr 2,000 / To Suspense A/c 2,000.
[TABLE]
Suspense A/c — Debit (Rs) | Suspense A/c — Credit (Rs)
To Difference in trial balance 5,000 | By Rent A/c 3,000
| By Purchases A/c 2,000
Total 5,000 | Total 5,000
[/TABLE]
• Effect on profit — Statement of corrected profit: Reported net profit; add the items wrongly charged or omitted income; less items wrongly credited or omitted expenses; = corrected net profit.
– Example: Reported profit Rs 40,000. Errors: (i) furniture purchase Rs 5,000 debited to Purchases (reduces profit, so add back 5,000); (ii) wages Rs 2,000 for installation debited to Wages (add back 2,000); (iii) Sales Rs 3,000 omitted (add 3,000); (iv) Rent Rs 1,000 not recorded (less 1,000). Corrected profit = 40,000 + 5,000 + 2,000 + 3,000 − 1,000 = Rs 49,000.
• Errors after final accounts: use Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c — affected nominal accounts are debited/credited to this account; its balance goes to capital.

notes.title: 7.1 Meaning and Need
notes.content:
• Bank reconciliation statement (BRS): a statement prepared to reconcile (agree) the balance as per the cash book (bank column) with the balance as per the pass book (bank statement) on a particular date, showing the reasons for the differences.
• Cash book (bank column): the customer's record of bank transactions. Pass book / bank statement: the bank's record of the customer's account — debit (Dr) = withdrawals; credit (Cr) = deposits. A favourable (credit) balance in the pass book means the customer has money; the debit balance in the pass book = overdraft. (Reverse in the cash book.)
• Need: to detect errors and fraud; to find items not yet recorded in the cash book (bank charges, interest, direct deposits, dishonoured cheques); to know the actual bank balance; to ensure the cash book is accurate; to ascertain the cheques outstanding; to avoid misappropriation; good internal control; required by auditors.
• Important: BRS is not an account — only a statement; it is prepared by the customer (business), not the bank. Timing differences will naturally resolve; errors need correction.

notes.title: 7.2 Reasons for Differences between Cash Book and Pass Book
notes.content:
• A. Timing differences (items in the cash book but not yet in the pass book):
– Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment (outstanding/ unpresented cheques) — cash book credited; bank not yet debited.
– Cheques deposited but not yet collected/ credited by the bank (cheques in clearing/ uncleared cheques) — cash book debited; bank not yet credited.
• B. Items in the pass book but not in the cash book:
– Bank charges, interest on overdraft, commission, cheque book charges, incidental charges — debited by bank.
– Interest on deposits, dividends collected by the bank directly — credited by bank.
– Direct deposit by a customer into the bank account; direct payments by the bank on standing instructions (insurance premium, EMI, subscriptions); bills collected by the bank on behalf of customer; NEFT/RTGS/UPI receipts or payments not yet recorded.
– Cheques dishonoured — debited by bank.
– Interest on drawings/ investments etc.
• C. Errors: errors committed by the business or the bank (wrong amount, wrong side, wrong totalling, omissions).
• D. Others: post-dated cheque — in the cash book but not yet presented; wrong credit by the bank (to another customer).

notes.title: 7.3 Preparing a BRS and Adjusting the Cash Book
notes.content:
• Two approaches:
– (1) Start with the balance as per the cash book and arrive at the pass book balance.
– (2) Start with the balance as per the pass book and arrive at the cash book balance.
• If the unadjusted cash book balance is the starting point (favourable balance):
[TABLE]
Item | Effect on cash book balance → pass book balance
Cheques issued but not presented | Add
Cheques deposited not yet collected | Less
Interest/ direct deposit credited by bank, not in CB | Add
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Item | Effect on cash book balance → pass book balance
Bank charges/ standing instruction payments debited by bank, not in CB | Less
[/TABLE]
• A reliable approach is to first update the cash book (adjust for items shown only in the pass book) to get the "adjusted cash book balance", then reconcile this with the pass book: Balance as per adjusted cash book + cheques issued not presented − cheques deposited not collected = Balance as per pass book.
• Rules (when starting from the favourable cash book balance):
– Add: cheques issued but not presented; interest/ dividend credited by bank; direct deposits by customers; bills collected by bank (not recorded in CB).
– Deduct: cheques deposited but not collected; bank charges; direct payments by the bank (insurance, EMI); cheques dishonoured.
• When starting from the overdrawn (unfavourable) balance, signs are reversed.
• Rules (starting from the favourable pass book balance): add cheques deposited but not collected; less cheques issued but not presented; less interest/ direct deposits credited by bank; add bank charges/ direct payments debited by bank.
• Illustration: Balance as per cash book Rs 25,000 (Dr). (i) Cheques issued Rs 5,000 not yet presented. (ii) Cheques deposited Rs 3,000 not yet collected. (iii) Bank charges Rs 200 debited by bank not in cash book. (iv) Interest Rs 500 credited by the bank not in cash book. (v) A customer deposited Rs 1,500 directly into the bank.
[TABLE]
Particulars | Rs
Balance as per Cash Book | 25,000
Add: Cheques issued but not yet presented | 5,000
Add: Interest credited by bank | 500
Add: Direct deposit by customer | 1,500
Less: Cheques deposited but not yet collected | (3,000)
Less: Bank charges | (200)
Balance as per Pass Book | 28,800
[/TABLE]
• Adjusted cash book: 25,000 + 500 + 1,500 − 200 = 26,800 → pass book balance = 26,800 + 5,000 − 3,000 = 28,800.
• Adjusting entries in the cash book: bank charges: Bank Charges A/c Dr. / To Bank; interest: Bank Dr. / To Interest received; direct deposit: Bank Dr. / To Customer; dishonour: Customer Dr. / To Bank.
• Overdraft example: Overdraft as per cash book Rs 8,000; cheque issued Rs 2,000 not presented; cheque deposited Rs 1,000 not collected: Overdraft as per pass book = 8,000 − 2,000 + 1,000 = Rs 7,000. (For an overdraft, cheques issued but not presented reduce the overdraft in the pass book; uncollected deposits increase it.)

notes.title: 7.4 Differences between Cash Book and Pass Book
notes.content:
[TABLE]
Basis | Cash Book | Pass Book
Prepared by | The business | The bank
Shows | Bank transactions as per the customer | Customer's account as per the bank
Deposits | Debit | Credit
Withdrawals | Credit | Debit
Favourable balance | Debit balance | Credit balance
Purpose | Record of transactions | Evidence of bank transactions
[/TABLE]

notes.group_name: Unit 8: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietorship
notes.title: 8.1 Final Accounts: Meaning and Components
notes.content:
• Final accounts (financial statements) are prepared at the end of the accounting year from the trial balance to find the profit or loss and the financial position.
• Components: (1) Trading Account — gross profit/ gross loss; (2) Profit and Loss Account — net profit/ net loss; (3) Balance Sheet — financial position on a given date.
• Objectives: to find gross profit, net profit, financial position; to help tax assessment and comparison; to help decision making and credit.
• Capital and revenue items: capital items (assets, liabilities, capital) go to the balance sheet; revenue items (incomes and expenses) go to trading/ P&L.

notes.group_name: Unit 8: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietorship
notes.title: 8.2 Trading Account
notes.content:
• Trading account: prepared to find the gross profit (GP) or gross loss from buying and selling (or manufacturing and selling) goods. GP = Net sales − Cost of goods sold (COGS).
• COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock. Net purchases = purchases − returns outward; net sales = sales − returns inward.
• Format (debit side): opening stock; purchases less purchase returns; direct expenses (wages, carriage inwards/ freight inwards, fuel/ power, factory expenses, import duty, octroi, dock charges, manufacturing expenses); gross profit c/d. Credit side: sales less sales returns; closing stock; gross loss c/d.
• Direct expenses are those incurred to bring goods to their present location and condition. Indirect expenses go to the P&L account.
• Closing entries (trading): Trading A/c Dr. / To Opening Stock, To Purchases, To Carriage inwards, To Wages…; Sales Dr. / To Trading A/c; Purchases Returns Dr. / To Trading; Closing Stock A/c Dr. / To Trading A/c; Trading A/c Dr. / To P&L A/c (gross profit).
• Gross profit ratio: (Gross profit ÷ Net sales) × 100.

notes.group_name: Unit 8: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietorship
notes.title: 8.3 Profit and Loss Account
notes.content:
• Profit and Loss Account: prepared to find the net profit/ net loss by considering all indirect expenses and incomes. Net profit = Gross profit + other incomes − indirect expenses (and losses).
• Debit side: indirect expenses — office and administrative expenses (salaries, rent, rates, taxes, insurance, stationery, printing, telephone, electricity, audit fees, legal fees), selling and distribution expenses (advertising, carriage outwards, commission to salesmen, godown rent, packing, bad debts), financial expenses (interest on loan, discount allowed, bank charges), depreciation, repairs, provision for doubtful debts, losses (loss by fire/theft), and gross loss b/d (if any).
• Credit side: gross profit b/d; other incomes — commission received, interest received, discount received, rent received, dividends, bad debts recovered, profit on sale of assets, provision for discount (if reduction).
• Net profit is transferred to Capital A/c (added); net loss — deducted from capital.
• Items not shown in P&L: drawings, income tax of the proprietor (personal), capital expenditure, interest on drawings is shown as an income (credit) and interest on capital as an expense (debit).
• Net profit ratio: (Net profit ÷ Net sales) × 100.

notes.group_name: Unit 8: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietorship
notes.title: 8.4 Balance Sheet
notes.content:
• Balance sheet: a statement of assets and liabilities at a given date showing the financial position. It is not an account — it is a statement; it has no debit or credit side (left side is "Liabilities", right side "Assets" in the traditional horizontal format).
• Marshalling of assets and liabilities: the order in which they are arranged — liquidity order (most liquid first: cash, bank, bills receivable, debtors, stock, prepaid expenses, investments, fixed assets) and permanence order (least liquid first — goodwill, land, building, machinery… cash last). For liabilities: order of permanence — capital, long-term loans, current liabilities. (Companies follow Schedule III vertical format.)
• Classification of assets: Fixed assets (tangible and intangible), current assets, investments, fictitious assets. Liabilities: capital, long-term liabilities (loans), current liabilities (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, income received in advance, bank overdraft).
• Capital account in balance sheet: Opening capital + Net profit + additional capital + interest on capital − drawings − interest on drawings − net loss = Closing capital.

notes.group_name: Unit 8: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietorship
notes.title: 8.5 Adjusting Entries
notes.content:
• Adjustments are required to follow the accrual and matching concepts. Each adjustment has a double effect — (i) in the Trading/P&L and (ii) in the balance sheet — if given outside the trial balance. If an adjustment is already in the trial balance, it has only a single effect (usually in the balance sheet or only P&L).
• Common adjustments:
[TABLE]
Adjustment | Treatment in P&L/Trading | Treatment in balance sheet
Closing stock | Credit side of trading A/c | Current asset
Outstanding expenses | Add to the expense | Current liability
Prepaid expenses | Deduct from the expense | Current asset
Accrued income | Add to income | Current asset
Income received in advance (unearned) | Deduct from income | Current liability
Depreciation | Debit to P&L | Deduct from the asset
Bad debts (further) | Add to bad debts in P&L | Deduct from debtors
Provision for doubtful debts (new) | Debit P&L (new − old) | Deduct from debtors
Provision for discount on debtors | Debit P&L | Deduct from debtors (after provision for bad debts)
Interest on capital | Debit P&L | Add to capital
Interest on drawings | Credit P&L | Deduct from capital
Goods withdrawn by the proprietor | Deduct from purchases (trading) | Deduct from capital
Loss of goods by fire (insured) | Loss by fire to P&L; claim as asset | Insurance claim receivable
Interest on loan outstanding | Add to interest paid | Current liability
Manager's commission | Debit P&L | Current liability
[/TABLE]
• Provision for doubtful debts: an estimate of bad debts expected on the existing debtors; created at a percentage of debtors after deducting further bad debts. P&L charge = new provision + bad debts − old provision (and bad debts recovered). If the new provision is less than the old provision, the excess is credited to P&L.
• Provision for discount on debtors: calculated on the good debtors (debtors − further bad debts − provision for bad debts).
• Reserve vs provision: provision is a charge against profit for a known liability or loss (compulsory); reserve is an appropriation of profit (voluntary).
• Closing entries (summary): transfer all nominal accounts to Trading and P&L A/c; net profit to capital; open accounts closed; balance sheet shows remaining balances.
• Opening entries for the next year: assets Dr / liabilities and capital Cr.

notes.title: 9.1 Meaning, Need and Causes of Depreciation
notes.content:
• Depreciation: the gradual and permanent decrease in the value of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time, obsolescence or other causes. AS 6/ Ind AS 16: "Depreciation is a measure of the wearing out, consumption or other loss of value of a depreciable asset arising from use, effluxion of time or obsolescence through technology and market changes."
• Features: it is a non-cash expense; applies to fixed (wasting) assets (machinery, building, furniture, vehicles, patents) — not to land (except mines), not to current assets; allocation of cost over useful life; charged every year even if there is no profit; it is a charge against profit.
• Related terms: Depletion (wasting of natural resources — mines, oil wells), Amortisation (writing off intangible assets — patents, goodwill), Fluctuation (market value change — not depreciation), Obsolescence (becoming out of date), Cost of the asset (purchase price + installation + freight + other expenses to bring the asset to use), Scrap/ residual (salvage) value, Useful life, Book value (written down value) = cost − accumulated depreciation. Depreciable amount = Cost − Scrap value.
• Need for depreciation: to ascertain true profit (matching concept); to show the true financial position (asset at its fair book value); to provide funds for replacement (retaining the profit if a depreciation fund is created); for tax reasons (allowed expense); to comply with law (Companies Act — Schedule II); to determine the true cost of production and product prices.
• Causes of depreciation:
– Internal: wear and tear (physical use), passage of time (efflux of time — leases, patents), exhaustion (mines/ quarries), accidents, depletion.
– External: obsolescence (technological change, new inventions, change in fashion/ demand), market conditions, legal restrictions, fall in market price (not a true cause).
• Factors affecting depreciation: cost of the asset, estimated useful life, estimated scrap value, additions (capital expenditure) during life, method of depreciation, the expected usage/ output, the asset's repairs and maintenance, technology changes.
• Difference between depreciation and other terms:
[TABLE]
Term | Meaning
Depreciation | Fall in value of tangible fixed assets
Depletion | Exhaustion of natural resources
Amortisation | Writing off of intangible assets
Fluctuation | Temporary change in market value
Obsolescence | A cause of depreciation (becoming outdated)
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 9.2 Methods of Depreciation — Straight Line Method and Written Down Value Method
notes.content:
• 1. Straight Line Method (SLM) / Fixed Instalment/ Original Cost Method: an equal amount is charged every year over the useful life.
– Annual depreciation = (Cost of the asset − Scrap value) ÷ Estimated useful life. Rate of depreciation = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100.
– Features: simple; depreciation is the same each year; book value falls in a straight line to scrap value; but the repair cost rises with age, so the total charge (depreciation + repairs) is unequal — a drawback.
– Suitable for: assets with a fixed life and little obsolescence — leases, patents, copyrights, buildings, furniture.
– Merits: simple, certain, asset can be written off to nil/ scrap value, widely used, accepted by tax in certain cases (companies). Demerits: ignores the effect of interest and repairs; ignores that an asset is more productive in early years; not realistic; difficult to estimate life and scrap.
• 2. Written Down Value Method (WDV)/ Diminishing Balance/ Reducing Balance Method: depreciation is charged at a fixed percentage on the book value (opening WDV) each year — it decreases every year; the asset never becomes nil.
– Depreciation for the year = Rate % × Opening book value.
– Merits: depreciation + repairs total tends to be uniform across years (higher depreciation in the early years when repairs are low); recognised by Income Tax law (for tax purposes, the WDV method with prescribed block rates is used); reflects greater usage/ obsolescence early; more realistic. Demerits: the asset never reaches zero; difficult to determine the suitable rate; the cost is not fully written off; extra complexity.
• Other methods (for awareness): Sum of Years' Digits, Annuity method, Depreciation fund (sinking fund) method, Insurance policy method, Revaluation method (for small tools/ livestock), Units of Production (Machine hour rate) method — depreciation = (cost − scrap) × (units produced ÷ total expected units), Depletion method (for mines).
• Illustration — Machine bought on 1 April 2023 for Rs 1,00,000; scrap value Rs 10,000; life 5 years.
– SLM: (1,00,000 − 10,000) ÷ 5 = Rs 18,000 per year. (Book value at the end of year 3 = 1,00,000 − 54,000 = Rs 46,000.)
– WDV at 20%:
[TABLE]
Year | Opening WDV (Rs) | Depreciation @20% (Rs) | Closing WDV (Rs)
1 | 1,00,000 | 20,000 | 80,000
2 | 80,000 | 16,000 | 64,000
3 | 64,000 | 12,800 | 51,200
4 | 51,200 | 10,240 | 40,960
5 | 40,960 | 8,192 | 32,768
[/TABLE]
• SLM vs WDV:
[TABLE]
Basis | Straight Line Method | Written Down Value Method
Depreciation | Same each year | Reduces each year
Base | Original cost | Opening book value
Book value | Falls to scrap value/ zero | Never zero
Total charge incl. repairs | Increases over time | Tends to be even
Tax | Not generally for income tax | Accepted for income tax (block of assets)
Suitable for | Leases, patents, buildings | Machinery, vehicles
[/TABLE]
• Depreciation for part of the year: charged for the period of use (pro rata, e.g. months) on additions during the year; for assets sold, depreciation up to the date of sale.
• Under the Companies Act, 2013 (Schedule II): depreciation is based on useful lives (e.g. buildings 60 years, general plant 15 years, computers 3 years, vehicles 8 years, furniture 10 years) with residual value normally not more than 5% of cost.

notes.title: 9.3 Accounting Treatment of Depreciation
notes.content:
• Method 1 — By charging depreciation directly to the asset account (without provision for depreciation account): the asset appears in the books at book value.
– Journal entry: Depreciation A/c Dr. / To Asset A/c. Then: Profit and Loss A/c Dr. / To Depreciation A/c. The asset account shows a reducing balance each year; in the balance sheet: the asset at WDV.
• Method 2 — By creating a Provision for Depreciation (Accumulated Depreciation) Account: the asset account is maintained at original cost; the depreciation is accumulated in the Provision for Depreciation A/c.
– Entries: Depreciation A/c Dr. / To Provision for Depreciation A/c; and P&L A/c Dr. / To Depreciation A/c. In the balance sheet: Asset (at cost) less Provision for depreciation (accumulated) = net book value.
• Sale of an asset — treatment:
– Under Method 1: depreciation is charged up to the date of sale; the book value is compared with the sale price. Profit (sale price > book value) — credit to P&L; loss (sale price < book value) — debit to P&L.
• --- Entries: Cash/Bank Dr. (sale price); Loss on sale Dr. (if any) / To Asset A/c (book value); To Profit on sale (if any).
– Under Method 2: Asset Disposal A/c (Machinery Sale A/c): debit — asset at cost; credit — provision for depreciation on that asset and sale proceeds; the balance is profit or loss.
• --- Entries: Asset Disposal A/c Dr. / To Asset A/c (cost); Provision for Depreciation A/c Dr. / To Asset Disposal A/c (accumulated depreciation on the asset sold); Cash Dr. / To Asset Disposal A/c (sale price); P&L A/c Dr./ Cr. and Asset Disposal A/c Cr./ Dr. for the balancing figure.
• Illustration — Method 1 (WDV @ 20%) as above: The machine is sold at the end of year 3 for Rs 55,000. Book value = Rs 51,200. Profit = 55,000 − 51,200 = Rs 3,800. Entry: Bank Dr. 55,000 / To Machinery A/c 51,200; To Profit on sale of machinery A/c 3,800.
• Illustration — Method 2 (SLM, cost Rs 1,00,000): The machine is sold at the end of year 3 for Rs 40,000; accumulated depreciation (3 × 18,000) = 54,000; book value = 46,000; loss = 6,000. Asset Disposal A/c: Dr: To Machinery 1,00,000; Cr: By Provision for depreciation 54,000; By Bank 40,000; By P&L (loss) 6,000. Total 1,00,000 each side.
• Ledger of asset (Method 1) — SLM: Machinery A/c: Dr: To Bank 1,00,000 (Year 1) | Cr: By Depreciation 18,000; By Balance c/d 82,000. Year 2: To Balance b/d 82,000 | By Depreciation 18,000; By Balance c/d 64,000, etc.
• Illustration — Additions during the year: A machine costing Rs 1,00,000 (purchased 1 April 2024). Another machine of Rs 60,000 purchased on 1 October 2024. Depreciation @10% SLM, year ended 31 March 2025: machine 1 = 10,000; machine 2 = 60,000 × 10% × 6/12 = 3,000; total 13,000.
• Change of method (AS 6): permitted only if required by law/ accounting standard or if the change gives a better presentation. Retrospective computation — the difference (excess or deficiency) for past years is adjusted in the year of change and disclosed.
• Effects of depreciation: reduces profit (non-cash charge); retains funds in business; reduces book value; reduces tax liability. Depreciation does not itself provide funds unless profits are retained/invested.
• Ind AS 16 (PPE) and AS 10: components approach; useful life and residual value reviewed at least annually; depreciation begins when the asset is available for use; the cost model or revaluation model.
• Distinction: depreciation vs repairs: depreciation relates to the use and life of the asset (non-cash); repairs are actual cash costs to maintain the asset.
